questions.q: The scientific name of mango is Mangifera ______.
questions.e: In binomial nomenclature, Mangifera is the genus and indica is the specific epithet of mango.

questions.q: The basic unit of classification is ______.
questions.e: Species is the basic taxonomic category; it is a group of individuals with fundamental similarities.

questions.q: Which taxonomic category groups the genera Panthera (lion, tiger) and Felis (cat) together?
questions.e: Panthera and Felis are both placed in the family Felidae; a family is a group of related genera.

questions.q: Which taxonomic aid contains information on any one taxon only, such as a single family or genus?
questions.e: A monograph covers one taxon, while a flora covers the plants of an area and a manual helps identify species of an area.

questions.q: The five kingdom classification was proposed by ______.
questions.e: R.H. Whittaker (1969) proposed the kingdoms Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

questions.q: Fungi commonly known as sac fungi belong to the class ______.
questions.e: Ascomycetes produce sexual spores called ascospores inside sac-like asci, hence the name sac fungi.

questions.q: Organisms that completely lack a cell wall, are the smallest living cells known and can survive without oxygen are ______.
questions.e: Mycoplasma lack a cell wall, are the smallest known living cells and many are pathogenic in plants and animals.

questions.q: Viroids, discovered by T.O. Diener, are free RNA that lack the ______ coat found in viruses.
questions.e: A virus has nucleic acid enclosed in a protein coat (capsid), but a viroid is only free RNA of low molecular weight.

questions.q: Diatomaceous earth, used in polishing and filtration of oils and syrups, is formed from the cell walls of which protists?
questions.e: Diatoms have silica-containing cell walls that do not decay easily, so their deposits form diatomaceous earth.

questions.q: In bryophytes, the main plant body is the haploid ______.
questions.e: The dominant plant body of bryophytes is the haploid gametophyte; the sporophyte is attached to it.

questions.q: In the moss life cycle, the first stage of the gametophyte that develops directly from a spore is a creeping, green, branched, filamentous ______.
questions.e: A moss spore germinates into the protonema, from which the leafy stage of the gametophyte develops.

questions.q: Red algae owe their red colour to the pigment ______.
questions.e: Rhodophyceae have abundant r-phycoerythrin, which gives them their red colour.

questions.q: In brown algae, the food is stored as mannitol and ______.
questions.e: Phaeophyceae store food as complex carbohydrates such as laminarin or mannitol.

questions.q: The egg cell of an angiosperm has 12 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will be present in each endosperm cell?
questions.e: The endosperm is triploid (3n) as it forms from the fusion of a male gamete with two polar nuclei, so 3 × 12 = 36.

questions.q: Animals having a body cavity lined by mesoderm are called ______.
questions.e: A true coelom is a body cavity lined by mesoderm; animals possessing it are coelomates, such as annelids and chordates.

questions.q: The water vascular system is a characteristic feature of phylum ______.
questions.e: Echinoderms such as starfish use a water vascular system for locomotion, capture of food and respiration.

questions.q: Stinging cells called cnidoblasts, used for anchorage, defence and capture of prey, are found in phylum ______.
questions.e: Cnidarians like Hydra and jellyfish have cnidoblasts on their tentacles and body.

questions.q: An animal has a notochord present only in the larval tail. To which subphylum of chordates does it belong?
questions.e: In urochordates like Ascidia, the notochord is present only in the larval tail, whereas in cephalochordates it runs from head to tail throughout life.

questions.q: Meera found an animal in a pond that has moist skin without scales, a three-chambered heart and lays eggs in water.
p: (a) To which class does it belong?
Amphibia|amphibians|amphibian
(b) How many chambers does the heart of a crocodile have?
(c) The common chamber into which the alimentary canal, urinary and reproductive tracts open in amphibians is called the ______.
cloaca
questions.e: Amphibians have moist scaleless skin, a three-chambered heart and a cloaca; crocodiles are the reptiles with a four-chambered heart.

questions.q: In pea, leaflets are modified into thread-like structures for climbing called ______.
questions.e: In pea, some leaflets are modified into tendrils that coil around supports to help the plant climb.

questions.q: The placentation in which ovules are borne on a central axis in a multilocular ovary, as in China rose, tomato and lemon, is ______ placentation.
questions.e: In axile placentation the placenta is axial and the ovules are attached to it in a multilocular ovary.

questions.q: In family Fabaceae, the corolla consisting of a standard, two wings and a keel is called ______.
questions.e: Fabaceae flowers (like pea) have a papilionaceous corolla with vexillary aestivation.

questions.q: In plants like Rhizophora growing in swampy areas, many roots come out of the ground and grow vertically upwards to get oxygen. These roots are called ______.
questions.e: Pneumatophores are negatively geotropic roots that help mangrove plants obtain oxygen for respiration.

questions.q: The cell theory was formulated by Schleiden and ______.
questions.e: Matthias Schleiden and Theodore Schwann together formulated the cell theory; Virchow later modified it.

questions.q: A prokaryotic 70S ribosome is made of two subunits. What is the size of the larger subunit (in Svedberg units)?
questions.e: A 70S ribosome consists of a 50S and a 30S subunit; S values are not additive because they depend on shape as well as size.

questions.q: Rudolf Virchow explained that cells divide and new cells are formed from pre-existing cells: Omnis cellula-e ______.
questions.e: Virchow's statement Omnis cellula-e cellula gave the cell theory its final shape.

questions.q: Membrane-bound vesicles formed by the Golgi apparatus that are rich in hydrolytic enzymes are called ______.
questions.e: Lysosomes contain hydrolases (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) that are active at acidic pH.

questions.q: A chromosome has its centromere close to one end, forming one extremely short and one very long arm. It is called a(n) ______ chromosome.
questions.e: In acrocentric chromosomes the centromere is near the end; in telocentric ones it is at the terminal end.

questions.q: The phase of the cell cycle between two successive M phases is called ______.
questions.e: Interphase (G1, S and G2) is the preparatory phase that lasts more than 95% of the cell cycle.

questions.q: Crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes takes place during the ______ stage of prophase I.
questions.e: Crossing over occurs in pachytene; the chiasmata formed become visible in diplotene.

questions.q: The stage of mitosis in which chromosome morphology is most easily studied, with all chromosomes lying at the equator, is ______.
questions.e: At metaphase, condensed chromosomes align on the metaphase plate, making them ideal for study.

questions.q: A diploid cell has 16 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will each daughter cell have at the end of meiosis I?
questions.e: Meiosis I is reductional: homologous chromosomes separate, so each daughter cell gets 8 chromosomes (each with two chromatids).

questions.q: A cell in G1 phase has 2C DNA content and 20 chromosomes.
p: (a) What will be its DNA content after S phase (in C)?
C
(b) How many chromosomes will it have after S phase?
(c) How many chromosomes will each cell have at the end of meiosis II?
questions.e: DNA doubles in S phase but chromosome number stays the same; meiosis halves the chromosome number to 10 in the final cells.

questions.q: The first stable product of the Calvin cycle (C3 pathway) is ______.
questions.e: CO2 combines with RuBP to form two molecules of the 3-carbon compound 3-PGA.

questions.q: The enzyme that catalyses the carboxylation of RuBP in the Calvin cycle is ______.
questions.e: RuBisCO is the most abundant enzyme in the world and fixes CO2 to RuBP.

questions.q: In C4 plants, the primary CO2 acceptor in mesophyll cells is ______.
questions.e: PEP (a 3-carbon molecule) accepts CO2 with the help of the enzyme PEPcase to form oxaloacetic acid.

questions.q: The special leaf anatomy of C4 plants with large bundle sheath cells around vascular bundles is called ______ anatomy.
questions.e: Kranz means wreath, reflecting the arrangement of bundle sheath cells around the vascular bundles.

questions.q: How many molecules of ATP are required to make one molecule of glucose through the Calvin cycle?
questions.e: Each CO2 fixed needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH; 6 CO2 are fixed per glucose, so 6 × 3 = 18 ATP.

questions.q: Glycolysis takes place in the ______ of the cell.
questions.e: Glycolysis (EMP pathway) occurs in the cytoplasm of all living organisms.

questions.q: What is the respiratory quotient (RQ) when carbohydrates are completely oxidised?
questions.e: For glucose, 6 CO2 are released and 6 O2 consumed, so RQ = 6/6 = 1.

questions.q: For the fat tripalmitin: 2 C51H98O6 + 145 O2 gives 102 CO2 + 98 H2O + energy. Calculate the RQ (to one decimal place).
questions.e: RQ = CO2 evolved / O2 consumed = 102/145 = 0.7.

questions.q: Consider the complete aerobic respiration of one molecule of glucose.
p: (a) Name the first product of the Krebs cycle formed by condensation of acetyl CoA with oxaloacetic acid.
citric acid|citrate
(b) What is the final acceptor of electrons in the electron transport system?
oxygen|O2|molecular oxygen
(c) How many molecules of pyruvic acid are formed from one glucose in glycolysis?
questions.e: Glycolysis gives 2 pyruvate; acetyl CoA joins OAA to form citric acid, and oxygen finally accepts electrons to form water.

questions.q: The cartilaginous flap that covers the glottis during swallowing to prevent food from entering the larynx is the ______.
questions.e: The epiglottis closes the glottis while swallowing so that food goes into the oesophagus.

questions.q: The tidal volume of a healthy man is approximately ______ mL.
questions.e: Tidal volume is the volume of air inspired or expired during normal respiration, about 500 mL.

questions.q: A person has tidal volume 500 mL, inspiratory reserve volume 2500 mL and expiratory reserve volume 1000 mL. Calculate the vital capacity.
questions.e: Vital capacity = ERV + TV + IRV = 1000 + 500 + 2500 = 4000 mL.

questions.q: Arjun's spirometry readings are: TV 500 mL, ERV 1100 mL, RV 1200 mL and IRV 3000 mL.
p: (a) Calculate his functional residual capacity.
mL
(b) Calculate his inspiratory capacity.
mL
(c) Calculate his total lung capacity.
mL
questions.e: FRC = ERV + RV = 2300 mL; IC = TV + IRV = 3500 mL; TLC = RV + ERV + TV + IRV = 5800 mL.

questions.q: The pacemaker of the human heart is the ______.
questions.e: The SA node generates the maximum number of action potentials per minute (70-75) and sets the rhythm of the heart.

questions.q: A person with blood group ______ can donate blood to persons of any ABO group and is called a universal donor.
questions.e: Group O red cells have neither antigen A nor B, so they are not agglutinated by recipients' antibodies.

questions.q: If the stroke volume is 70 mL and the heart rate is 72 beats per minute, calculate the cardiac output in mL per minute.
questions.e: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 70 × 72 = 5040 mL per minute (about 5 litres).

questions.q: Riya is Rh-negative and her husband is Rh-positive. Their first child is Rh-positive.
p: (a) Name the condition that may affect a second Rh-positive foetus.
erythroblastosis foetalis|erythroblastosis fetalis
(b) If the heart rate is 75 beats per minute, what is the duration of one cardiac cycle?
s
(c) Which are the most abundant cells in human blood?
RBCs|RBC|erythrocytes|red blood cells|erythrocyte
questions.e: Anti-Rh antibodies formed in the mother can destroy foetal RBCs in the next pregnancy; one cardiac cycle lasts 60/75 = 0.8 s.

questions.q: The hard outer layer of the pollen grain wall, made of sporopollenin, is called the ______.
questions.e: Exine is made of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials known; the inner wall is the intine.

questions.q: The innermost wall layer of the microsporangium, which nourishes the developing pollen grains, is the ______.
questions.e: Tapetal cells are dense, often multinucleate, and nourish the developing pollen grains.

questions.q: The megaspore mother cell of a flowering plant has 24 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are present in a synergid cell?
questions.e: The MMC is diploid; after meiosis the embryo sac cells, including synergids, are haploid, so 24 ÷ 2 = 12.

questions.q: Development of fruits without fertilisation, as in banana, is called ______.
questions.e: Parthenocarpic fruits are seedless; parthenocarpy can also be induced by growth hormones.

questions.q: Consider a typical mature angiosperm embryo sac (Polygonum type).
p: (a) How many nuclei does it contain?
(b) How many cells does it contain?
(c) What is the fusion of a male gamete with the two polar nuclei called?
triple fusion
questions.e: The embryo sac is 8-nucleate and 7-celled (the two polar nuclei share the central cell); triple fusion forms the triploid primary endosperm nucleus.

questions.q: In humans, fertilisation normally takes place in the ______ region of the fallopian tube.
questions.e: Fertilisation can occur only if the ovum and sperms reach the ampullary region of the fallopian tube at the same time.

questions.q: During pregnancy, the hormone hCG is secreted by the ______.
questions.e: The placenta acts as an endocrine tissue and produces hCG, hPL, oestrogens and progestogens.

questions.q: Cells in the interstitial spaces outside the seminiferous tubules that synthesise and secrete androgens are ______ cells.
questions.e: Leydig (interstitial) cells secrete androgens such as testosterone; Sertoli cells nourish germ cells.

questions.q: How many sperms will be formed from 25 primary spermatocytes?
questions.e: Each primary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis to form 4 spermatids, which become 4 sperms: 25 × 4 = 100.

questions.q: The foetal sex determination test based on analysing the chromosomal pattern in the amniotic fluid is called ______.
questions.e: Amniocentesis is meant to detect genetic disorders; its misuse for sex determination is banned in India.

questions.q: CuT, Cu7 and Multiload 375 are examples of ______-releasing IUDs.
questions.e: Cu ions released by these IUDs suppress sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms.

questions.q: In assisted reproductive technology, transfer of the zygote or early embryo (up to 8 blastomeres) into the fallopian tube is called ______.
questions.a: ZIFT|zygote intra fallopian transfer|zygote intrafallopian transfer
questions.e: In ZIFT the embryo is placed in the fallopian tube; embryos with more than 8 blastomeres are transferred into the uterus (IUT).

questions.q: Mendel conducted his hybridisation experiments on the garden ______.
questions.e: Mendel worked on garden pea (Pisum sativum) for seven years (1856-1863).

questions.q: In the F2 generation of a Mendelian dihybrid cross (ratio 9:3:3:1), how many plants out of 16 show both recessive traits?
questions.e: Only the double homozygous recessive (e.g. rryy) shows both recessive traits, which is 1 out of 16.

questions.q: In snapdragon, red (RR) crossed with white (rr) gives pink (Rr) flowers due to incomplete dominance. If 400 plants are raised in F2, how many are expected to be pink?
questions.e: The F2 ratio is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, so pink = 2/4 × 400 = 200.

questions.q: A woman with blood group O marries a man with blood group AB. What is the probability (in %) that their child will have blood group O?
questions.e: The mother gives only i and the father gives IA or IB, so children are IAi (A) or IBi (B); none can be O.

questions.q: Haemophilia is a sex-linked recessive disorder. A carrier woman marries a normal man.
p: (a) What percentage of their sons are likely to be haemophilic?
(b) What percentage of their daughters are likely to be haemophilic?
(c) On which chromosome is the haemophilia gene located?
X|X chromosome
questions.e: Sons get their X from the mother, so half are affected; daughters get a normal X from the father, so they are normal or carriers.

questions.q: The discontinuously synthesised fragments (Okazaki fragments) are joined by the enzyme DNA ______.
questions.e: DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand during replication.

questions.q: In RNA, the base thymine is replaced by ______.
questions.e: RNA contains uracil (5-demethylated thymine) in place of thymine.

questions.q: A double-stranded DNA sample contains 20% cytosine. What percentage of adenine does it contain?
questions.e: By Chargaff's rule C = G = 20%, so A + T = 60% and A = 30%.

questions.q: Meselson and Stahl proved semi-conservative replication by growing E. coli in a medium containing the heavy isotope of nitrogen, ______.
questions.e: DNA labelled with 15N is denser than 14N DNA, so hybrid DNA could be separated by CsCl density gradient centrifugation.

questions.q: The distance between two consecutive base pairs in B-DNA is 0.34 nm. What is the length of a DNA segment of 1000 base pairs (in nm)?
questions.e: Length = number of base pairs × 0.34 nm = 1000 × 0.34 = 340 nm.

questions.q: A template strand of DNA has the sequence 3'-TACGGA-5'.
p: (a) Write the mRNA transcribed from it (5' to 3').
AUGCCU|AUG CCU|5'-AUGCCU-3'|5' AUGCCU 3'
(b) Which amino acid does the first codon code for?
methionine|met
(c) Out of 64 codons, how many code for amino acids?
questions.e: mRNA is complementary to the template, giving AUG CCU; AUG codes for methionine and is the start codon; 3 of the 64 codons are stop codons.

questions.q: The theory of evolution by natural selection was proposed by Charles ______.
questions.e: Charles Darwin, based on his voyage on HMS Beagle, explained evolution through natural selection.

questions.q: Wings of a butterfly and of a bird perform the same function but are anatomically different. They are ______ organs.
questions.e: Analogous organs result from convergent evolution: similar function, different structure and origin.

questions.q: In England after industrialisation, dark-winged moths outnumbered white-winged moths on soot-covered tree trunks. This phenomenon is called industrial ______.
questions.e: Dark moths were camouflaged on dark trunks and escaped predators, an example of natural selection.

questions.q: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of recessive allele a (q) is 0.3. What is the frequency of heterozygotes (2pq)?
Typhoid fever is caused by the bacterium Salmonella ______.
questions.e: Salmonella typhi enters the small intestine through contaminated food and water; Widal test confirms typhoid.

questions.q: Malaria is caused by the protozoan ______.
questions.e: Different species of Plasmodium (vivax, malariae, falciparum) cause malaria; P. falciparum causes the most serious form.

questions.q: Plasmodium enters the human body through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito as ______.
questions.e: Sporozoites are the infectious form; they first multiply in liver cells and then attack RBCs.

questions.q: The yellowish colostrum secreted by the mother in the initial days of lactation contains abundant antibodies of type ______.
questions.e: IgA in colostrum protects the infant; this is an example of passive immunity.

questions.q: After entering the body, HIV replicates in macrophages and then attacks which type of lymphocytes, decreasing their number?
questions.a: helper T cells|helper T lymphocytes|helper T-lymphocytes|TH cells|T helper cells
questions.e: HIV destroys helper T-lymphocytes, which weakens the immune system and leads to AIDS.

questions.q: Answer the following about immunity and drugs.
p: (a) Which type of immunity is produced when a person is vaccinated?
active|active immunity|artificial active immunity
(b) How many polypeptide chains does an antibody molecule have?
(c) Name the drug obtained from the latex of the poppy plant that is a very effective sedative and painkiller.
morphine
questions.e: Vaccines make the body produce its own antibodies (active immunity); an antibody (H2L2) has 2 heavy and 2 light chains; morphine is an opioid from Papaver somniferum.

questions.q: Lactobacillus and other bacteria that convert milk into curd are commonly called ______.
questions.e: Lactic acid bacteria produce acids that coagulate and partially digest milk proteins, and also increase vitamin B12.

questions.q: The large holes in Swiss cheese are due to the large amount of CO2 produced by the bacterium ______.
questions.e: Propionibacterium sharmanii releases CO2 during ripening, creating holes in Swiss cheese.

questions.q: Cyclosporin A, used as an immunosuppressive agent in organ-transplant patients, is produced by the fungus ______.
questions.e: Trichoderma polysporum produces cyclosporin A; Monascus purpureus produces blood-cholesterol lowering statins.

questions.q: The bacterium used as a biocontrol agent to control butterfly caterpillars is Bacillus ______.
questions.e: Spores of Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) release a toxin in the caterpillar gut that kills it without harming other insects.

questions.q: Enzymes that cut DNA at specific recognition sequences are called restriction ______.
questions.e: Restriction endonucleases are the molecular scissors of genetic engineering.

questions.q: The first restriction endonuclease to be isolated was Hind ______.
questions.e: Hind II, isolated about five years after the discovery of restriction enzymes, always cuts DNA at a specific six base pair sequence.

questions.q: EcoRI recognises the palindromic sequence 5'-GAATTC-3'. Between which two bases does it cut each strand?
questions.e: EcoRI cuts between G and A on both strands, leaving single-stranded sticky ends.

questions.q: In agarose gel electrophoresis, negatively charged DNA fragments move towards the ______.
questions.e: DNA is negatively charged due to phosphate groups, so it moves towards the anode; smaller fragments move farther.

questions.q: Answer about cloning vectors used in recombinant DNA technology.
p: (a) The vector pBR322 has resistance genes for ampicillin and which other antibiotic?
tetracycline|tet
(b) Selection of recombinants by colour (blue/white) using beta-galactosidase is based on ______ inactivation.
insertional
(c) Name the plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens used as a vector for plants.
Ti|Ti plasmid|tumour inducing plasmid|tumor inducing plasmid
questions.e: pBR322 carries ampR and tetR; insertion into the lacZ gene inactivates beta-galactosidase giving white colonies; the Ti plasmid has been modified into a plant vector.

questions.q: The first transgenic cow, which produced milk containing human alpha-lactalbumin, was named ______.
questions.e: Rosie (1997) produced human protein-enriched milk, nutritionally more balanced for human babies.

questions.q: Golden rice is a genetically modified variety rich in ______.
questions.e: Golden rice has been engineered to produce beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.

questions.q: Infestation of tobacco roots by the nematode Meloidogyne incognita was prevented using a technique based on silencing a specific mRNA. This technique is called RNA ______.
questions.e: In RNAi, nematode-specific genes were introduced to produce dsRNA that silences the parasite's mRNA, killing it.

questions.q: In 1983, Eli Lilly prepared chains A and B of human insulin separately in E. coli and then combined them. What type of bridges link chains A and B in insulin?
questions.e: The A and B chains of insulin are linked together by disulphide bridges.

questions.q: The interaction in which one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited is called ______.
questions.e: An orchid growing on a mango branch is an example of commensalism.

questions.q: The logistic (Verhulst-Pearl) growth curve of a population is ______-shaped.
questions.e: With limited resources, growth slows as the population nears carrying capacity, giving a sigmoid curve.

questions.q: A pond had 20 lotus plants last year; through reproduction 8 new plants were added this year. Calculate the birth rate (per lotus per year).
questions.e: Birth rate = 8 ÷ 20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year.

questions.q: A laboratory population of 80 frogs is studied; 4 frogs died during a week.
p: (a) Calculate the death rate (per frog per week).
(b) The equation dN/dt = rN describes which type of population growth?
exponential|exponential growth|geometric
(c) The maximum population size that an environment can support is called its ______.
carrying capacity|K
questions.e: Death rate = 4 ÷ 80 = 0.05; unlimited resources give exponential growth, while limited resources cap a population at its carrying capacity K.

questions.q: The tissue that covers body surfaces and lines body cavities, ducts and tubes is called ______ tissue.
questions.e: Epithelial tissue has a free surface facing a body fluid or the outside environment and provides a covering or lining for parts of the body.

questions.q: The most abundant and widely distributed tissue in the body of complex animals is ______ tissue.
questions.e: Connective tissues are the most abundant and widely distributed; they link and support other tissues and organs.

questions.q: When a frog is in water, it respires through its moist skin. This is called ______ respiration.
questions.e: In water the frog's skin acts as the respiratory organ (cutaneous respiration); on land the buccal cavity, skin and lungs are used.

questions.q: The inner surface of hollow organs such as bronchioles and fallopian tubes is lined by ______ epithelium.
questions.e: Columnar or cuboidal cells bearing cilia form ciliated epithelium; the cilia move particles or mucus in a specific direction, as in bronchioles and fallopian tubes.

questions.q: Which type of cell junction helps to stop substances from leaking across a tissue?
questions.e: Tight junctions stop leakage across a tissue; adhering junctions cement neighbouring cells, and gap junctions connect the cytoplasm of adjoining cells.

questions.q: Frogs excrete urea as their main nitrogenous waste, so they are ______ animals.
questions.e: The frog's excretory system eliminates nitrogenous waste mainly as urea, making it ureotelic.

questions.q: How many chambers does the heart of a frog have?
questions.e: The frog heart is three-chambered: two atria and one ventricle, covered by the pericardium.

questions.q: Cartilage, bone and blood are grouped as ______ connective tissues.
questions.e: NCERT classifies connective tissue into loose, dense and specialised types; cartilage, bones and blood are specialised connective tissues.

questions.q: In frog, the special venous connection between the kidneys and the lower parts of the body is called the ______ portal system.
questions.e: Frogs have a hepatic portal system (liver–intestine) and a renal portal system (kidney–lower body).

questions.q: In male frogs, the 10–12 vasa efferentia arising from the testes enter the kidneys and open into ______, which communicates with the urinogenital duct.
questions.e: Vasa efferentia enter the kidneys and open into Bidder's canal, which finally communicates with the urinogenital duct opening into the cloaca.

questions.q: Proteins are polymers (heteropolymers) of ______.
questions.e: Proteins are polypeptides, i.e. linear chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds.

questions.q: The most abundant protein in the animal world is ______.
questions.e: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the animal world; RuBisCO is the most abundant protein in the whole biosphere.

questions.q: The storage polysaccharide of animals, a polymer of glucose, is ______.
questions.e: Animals store glucose as glycogen; plants store it as starch.

questions.q: Inulin is a polymer of ______.
questions.e: Inulin is a polysaccharide made of fructose units.

questions.q: In a polysaccharide, the individual monosaccharides are linked by a ______ bond.
questions.e: Monosaccharides are joined by glycosidic bonds formed by dehydration between two carbon atoms of adjacent sugars.

questions.q: Fatty acids that have no double bonds in their hydrocarbon chain are called ______ fatty acids.
questions.e: Saturated fatty acids lack C=C double bonds; unsaturated ones have one or more.

questions.q: How many carbon atoms (including the carboxyl carbon) does palmitic acid have?
questions.e: Palmitic acid has 16 carbons including the carboxyl carbon; arachidonic acid has 20.

questions.q: Nucleic acids that behave like enzymes are called ______.
questions.e: Almost all enzymes are proteins, but some nucleic acids (RNA) act as catalysts; these are ribozymes.

questions.q: Enzymes that catalyse the removal of groups from substrates by mechanisms other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds, belong to the class ______.
questions.e: Lyases remove groups from substrates by non-hydrolytic means, leaving double bonds.

questions.q: Malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase because it closely resembles the substrate succinate. This is ______ inhibition.
questions.e: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the active site; malonate inhibiting succinic dehydrogenase is the classic example.

questions.q: Kinetin, first isolated from autoclaved herring sperm DNA, belongs to which group of plant growth regulators?
questions.e: Kinetin (a modified adenine) was discovered by Skoog and Miller as a cytokinin; it promotes cell division (cytokinesis).

questions.q: The only gaseous plant growth regulator is ______.
questions.e: Ethylene is a simple gaseous PGR that promotes fruit ripening, senescence and abscission.

questions.q: The plant growth regulator called the 'stress hormone' is ______.
questions.e: ABA increases tolerance of plants to stresses and stimulates stomatal closure, so it is called the stress hormone.

questions.q: Gibberellins were discovered from the fungus Gibberella fujikuroi, which causes the ______ disease of rice seedlings.
questions.e: E. Kurosawa reported that sterile filtrates of Gibberella fujikuroi produced the symptoms of bakanae (foolish seedling) disease in healthy rice seedlings.

questions.q: Decapitation (removal of shoot tips) is used in tea plantations and hedge-making to overcome apical dominance caused by ______.
questions.e: The growing apical bud, through auxin, inhibits lateral buds (apical dominance); removing it lets lateral branches grow.

questions.q: The phenomenon by which living differentiated cells that had lost the capacity to divide regain it is called ______.
questions.e: Formation of interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from fully differentiated cells is an example of dedifferentiation.

questions.q: In arithmetic growth, a plot of length against time gives a ______ curve.
questions.e: In arithmetic growth only one daughter cell continues dividing, giving a constant rate and a linear curve (Lt = L0 + rt).

questions.q: The most widely used compound as a source of ethylene, which releases ethylene slowly when sprayed as an aqueous solution, is ______.
questions.e: Ethephon is absorbed and translocated within the plant and releases ethylene slowly; it hastens fruit ripening and flower/fruit thinning.

questions.q: Plants such as cotton, coriander and larkspur produce different kinds of leaves in juvenile and mature stages. This ability to follow different pathways in response to environment or phases of life is called ______.
questions.e: Heterophylly is an example of plasticity, the ability of plants to form different structures in response to environment or life phase.

questions.q: Spraying sugarcane with gibberellins increases stem length and raises the yield by as much as how many tonnes per acre?
questions.e: Since sugarcane stores sugar in its stem, GA-induced stem elongation increases yield by as much as 20 tonnes per acre.

questions.q: The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the ______.
questions.e: Each human kidney has nearly one million nephrons, the functional units of the kidney.

questions.q: Reptiles, birds, land snails and insects excrete nitrogenous wastes mainly as ______.
questions.e: These animals are uricotelic, excreting uric acid as pellets or paste with minimum loss of water.

questions.q: Which hormone, released from the neurohypophysis, facilitates water reabsorption from the latter parts of the renal tubule and prevents diuresis?
questions.e: ADH (vasopressin) increases water reabsorption from the DCT and collecting duct, preventing diuresis.

questions.q: What is the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in a healthy human, in ml per minute?
questions.e: On average about 125 ml of filtrate is formed per minute by the kidneys, i.e. about 180 litres per day.

questions.q: The juxtaglomerular apparatus is formed by cellular modifications in the distal convoluted tubule and the ______ at their point of contact.
questions.e: JGA is a sensitive region where the DCT contacts the afferent arteriole; it regulates GFR by releasing renin.

questions.q: The epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule, which are arranged to leave minute filtration slits, are called ______.
questions.e: Podocytes of the Bowman's capsule leave filtration slits (slit pores) through which blood is filtered.

questions.q: About how many litres of glomerular filtrate are formed in human kidneys per day?
questions.e: 125 ml/min × 1440 min ≈ 180 litres per day; only about 1.5 litres is excreted as urine, so nearly 99% is reabsorbed.

questions.q: Besides NaCl, which substance, partly re-entering the thin ascending limb from the collecting tubule, helps maintain the concentration gradient in the medullary interstitium?
questions.e: Small amounts of urea enter the thin segment of the ascending limb and are transported back to the interstitium by the collecting tubule, helping maintain the gradient.

questions.q: The counter-current mechanism produces an osmolarity gradient from 300 mOsmolL⁻¹ in the cortex to about how many mOsmolL⁻¹ in the inner medulla?
questions.e: The gradient rises from 300 mOsmolL⁻¹ in the cortex to about 1200 mOsmolL⁻¹ in the inner medulla, allowing concentrated urine.

questions.q: An increase in blood flow to the atria of the heart causes release of ______, which causes vasodilation and acts as a check on the renin–angiotensin mechanism.
questions.e: Atrial natriuretic factor decreases blood pressure by vasodilation, opposing the renin–angiotensin system.

questions.q: How many bones are there in the skeletal system of an adult human?
questions.e: The adult human skeleton has 206 bones: 80 in the axial and 126 in the appendicular skeleton.

questions.q: The portion of a myofibril between two successive Z-lines, considered the functional unit of contraction, is the ______.
questions.e: A sarcomere lies between two successive Z-lines and is the functional unit of muscle contraction.

questions.q: According to NCERT, the human skull is made up of a total of how many bones (cranial + facial)?
questions.e: The skull has 8 cranial bones and 14 facial bones, totalling 22.

questions.q: The last two pairs (11th and 12th) of ribs, which are not connected ventrally, are called ______ ribs.
questions.e: The first 7 pairs are true ribs, the 8th–10th are false (vertebrochondral) ribs, and the 11th–12th are floating ribs.

questions.q: During muscle contraction, Ca²⁺ binds to a subunit of ______ on the actin filament, removing the masking of the active sites for myosin.
questions.e: Increased Ca²⁺ binds troponin, unmasking actin's active sites so myosin heads can form cross bridges.

questions.q: Which autoimmune disorder affects the neuromuscular junction, leading to fatigue, weakening and paralysis of skeletal muscle?
questions.e: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction.

questions.q: How many bones make up the axial skeleton of humans?
questions.e: The axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, sternum, ribs) has 80 bones; the appendicular skeleton has 126.

questions.q: How many cervical vertebrae are present in humans (and almost all mammals)?
questions.e: There are 7 cervical vertebrae in almost all mammals including humans; there are 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar.

questions.q: The light bands of a myofibril, which contain only actin, are called ______.
questions.e: Light bands contain actin and are called I-bands (isotropic); dark A-bands (anisotropic) contain myosin.

questions.q: The joint between the atlas and axis vertebrae is a ______ joint.
questions.e: NCERT gives the atlas–axis joint as an example of a pivot joint (a synovial joint).

questions.q: The tract of nerve fibres that connects the left and right cerebral hemispheres is the ______.
questions.e: The cerebrum is divided into two hemispheres connected by the corpus callosum.

questions.q: The junction through which a nerve impulse is transmitted from one neuron to another is called a ______.
questions.e: A synapse is formed by the membranes of a pre-synaptic and a post-synaptic neuron; it may be electrical or chemical.

questions.q: In a myelinated nerve fibre, the gaps between two adjacent myelin sheaths are called ______.
questions.a: nodes of Ranvier|node of Ranvier|Ranvier's nodes
questions.e: Myelin sheaths are interrupted at the nodes of Ranvier, where the impulse jumps (saltatory conduction).

questions.q: Myelinated nerve fibres of the peripheral nervous system are enveloped by ______ cells, which form the myelin sheath.
questions.e: Schwann cells form the myelin sheath around the axon of myelinated fibres.

questions.q: Bipolar neurons, with one axon and one dendrite, are found in the ______ of the eye.
questions.e: NCERT: bipolar neurons are found in the retina; multipolar in the cerebral cortex; unipolar in the embryonic stage.

questions.q: The sodium-potassium pump transports how many Na⁺ ions outwards for every 2 K⁺ ions into the cell?
questions.e: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves 3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in, maintaining the ionic gradients of the resting membrane.

questions.q: Which part of the forebrain contains centres that control body temperature and the urge for eating and drinking?
questions.e: The hypothalamus, at the base of the thalamus, controls body temperature, eating and drinking, and also secretes hypothalamic hormones.

questions.q: The midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata together form the ______.
questions.e: Midbrain and hindbrain (pons and medulla) form the brain stem, connecting the brain to the spinal cord.

questions.q: The dorsal portion of the midbrain consists mainly of four round swellings called the ______.
questions.e: The dorsal midbrain has four round swellings (lobes) called corpora quadrigemina.

questions.q: At rest, the axonal membrane is comparatively more permeable to which ion?
questions.e: The resting axonal membrane is more permeable to K⁺ and nearly impermeable to Na⁺, so the axoplasm has high K⁺ and the inside is negative.

questions.q: The pineal gland secretes the hormone ______.
questions.e: Melatonin regulates the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm of the body, such as the sleep-wake cycle.

questions.q: Which hormone from the β-cells of the pancreas lowers blood glucose (hypoglycemic hormone)?
questions.e: Insulin promotes cellular glucose uptake and glycogenesis; glucagon from α-cells is hyperglycemic.

questions.q: Adrenaline and noradrenaline, called the 'emergency hormones', are secreted by the adrenal ______.
questions.e: The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines (adrenaline and noradrenaline) rapidly in response to stress or emergency.

questions.q: Deficiency of iodine in the diet results in hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid gland, commonly called ______.
questions.e: Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis; its deficiency causes hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid (goitre).

questions.q: Parathyroid hormone increases Ca²⁺ levels in the blood, so it is a ______ hormone.
questions.e: PTH stimulates bone resorption, Ca²⁺ reabsorption by renal tubules and Ca²⁺ absorption from digested food, raising blood Ca²⁺.

questions.q: The thymus secretes peptide hormones called ______, which play a major role in differentiation of T-lymphocytes.
questions.e: Thymosins help differentiate T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity) and promote antibody production (humoral immunity).

questions.q: In the human body, the main glucocorticoid is ______.
questions.e: Cortisol is the main glucocorticoid; aldosterone is the main mineralocorticoid.

questions.q: Underproduction of hormones by the adrenal cortex alters carbohydrate metabolism, causing acute weakness and fatigue. This disease is called ______.
questions.e: NCERT: underproduction of adrenal cortex hormones leads to Addison's disease.

questions.q: Which hypothalamic hormone inhibits the release of growth hormone from the pituitary?
questions.e: Hypothalamic hormones may be releasing or inhibiting; somatostatin from the hypothalamus inhibits growth hormone release.

questions.q: The pars intermedia of the pituitary secretes only one hormone, which acts on melanocytes and regulates skin pigmentation. Name it.
questions.e: Pars intermedia secretes MSH (melanocyte stimulating hormone); in humans it is almost merged with pars distalis.

questions.q: The vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels in an ecosystem (e.g. trees at the top, shrubs below, herbs and grasses at the bottom) is called ______.
questions.e: NCERT describes this vertical layering of species in an ecosystem, such as a forest, as stratification.

questions.q: The ecological pyramid of ______ is always upright and can never be inverted.
questions.e: Energy is lost as heat at every trophic level, so each higher level always has less energy; the pyramid of energy is therefore always upright.

questions.q: In decomposition, the breaking down of detritus into smaller particles by detritivores such as earthworms is called ______.
questions.e: Fragmentation is the first step of decomposition, in which detritivores break detritus into smaller particles.

questions.q: During decomposition, water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts. This process is called ______.
questions.e: Leaching is the downward movement of water-soluble nutrients into the soil, where they are precipitated as unavailable salts.

questions.q: Plants capture only 2–10 per cent of the ______ (the part of sunlight usable in photosynthesis, less than 50% of incident solar radiation).
questions.e: Less than 50% of incident solar radiation is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), and plants capture only 2–10% of PAR.

questions.q: The gross primary productivity of an ecosystem is 1000 kcal/m²/yr and respiration losses of the producers are 300 kcal/m²/yr. What is its net primary productivity?
questions.e: NPP = GPP − R = 1000 − 300 = 700 kcal/m²/yr.

questions.q: The producers of a food chain fix 20,000 J of energy. Using the 10 per cent law, how much energy is available to the secondary consumers?
questions.e: Only about 10% passes to each next trophic level: 20,000 J → 2,000 J (primary consumers) → 200 J (secondary consumers).

questions.q: According to NCERT, the annual net primary productivity of the whole biosphere is approximately how many billion tons (dry weight) of organic matter?
questions.e: Annual NPP of the biosphere is about 170 billion tons (dry weight); of this the oceans contribute only about 55 billion tons.

questions.q: The pyramid of biomass in the sea is generally inverted because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of ______.
questions.e: In the sea the producers (phytoplankton) have a small standing biomass, which is far exceeded by the biomass of fishes, giving an inverted pyramid of biomass.

questions.q: In a terrestrial ecosystem, a much larger fraction of energy flows through the ______ food chain than through the grazing food chain.
questions.e: In aquatic ecosystems the grazing food chain is the major conduit of energy flow, but in terrestrial ecosystems a much larger fraction flows through the detritus food chain.

questions.q: The term 'biodiversity' was popularised by the sociobiologist ______.
questions.a: Edward Wilson|E. O. Wilson|Wilson|E O Wilson
questions.e: Edward Wilson popularised the term biodiversity to describe the combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation.

questions.q: The Amazon rain forest, called the 'lungs of the planet', produces roughly what percentage of the total oxygen in the Earth's atmosphere?
questions.e: NCERT states the Amazon forest produces, through photosynthesis, about 20 per cent of the total oxygen in the Earth's atmosphere.

questions.q: The introduction of the ______ into Lake Victoria in East Africa led to the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish.
questions.e: The Nile perch, an alien species introduced into Lake Victoria, eventually led to the extinction of over 200 cichlid fish species.

questions.q: The 'rivet popper hypothesis', which compares species in an ecosystem to rivets in an airplane, was proposed by the ecologist ______.
questions.e: Stanford ecologist Paul Ehrlich used the rivet popper analogy to explain how loss of species weakens an ecosystem.

questions.q: India has only 2.4% of the world's land area. What is its share (in %) of the global species diversity?
questions.e: India's share of global species diversity is an impressive 8.1%, making it one of the 12 mega diversity countries.

questions.q: How many biodiversity hotspots are there in the world in total, according to NCERT?
questions.e: The total number of biodiversity hotspots in the world is now 34; three of them (Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya) cover India.

questions.q: For a region the species–area relationship is S = C A^Z with Z = 0.2. If the area studied is increased 32 times, by what factor does the species richness increase?
According to the IUCN Red List (2004), how many species have been documented as becoming extinct in the last 500 years?
questions.e: The IUCN Red List (2004) documents 784 extinctions in the last 500 years: 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants.

questions.q: The German naturalist and geographer who observed that within a region species richness increases with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit, was ______.
questions.e: Alexander von Humboldt, during his explorations of South American jungles, gave the species–area relationship.

questions.q: When a host fish species becomes extinct, the unique parasites associated with it also become extinct. This cause of biodiversity loss is called ______.
questions.e: Co-extinction: when a species becomes extinct, the plant and animal species obligatorily associated with it (e.g. its parasites) also become extinct.

questions.q: The system of binomial nomenclature was given by ______.
questions.e: Each organism has a two-part name: the genus followed by the specific epithet.

questions.q: In a scientific name such as Mangifera indica, the first word is the name of the ______.
questions.e: The first word (genus) starts with a capital letter; the second (specific epithet) with a small letter.

questions.q: The sum total of all the chemical reactions taking place in the body is called ______.
questions.e: All living organisms show metabolism; it is a defining feature of life.

questions.q: The ability of organisms to sense their surroundings and respond to them is called ______.
questions.e: NCERT describes consciousness as the most obvious and technically complicated feature of living organisms.

questions.q: Biological names are generally in ______ and are written in italics.
questions.e: They are Latinised or derived from Latin, whatever their origin.

questions.q: Which taxonomic category comes between genus and order?
questions.e: The hierarchy is kingdom, phylum/division, class, order, family, genus, species.

questions.q: In Homo sapiens, the word sapiens is the ______ epithet.
questions.e: Homo is the genus and sapiens is the specific epithet.

questions.q: Which is the highest taxonomic category?
questions.e: All plants are grouped in kingdom Plantae and all animals in kingdom Animalia.

questions.q: In plants, the category equivalent to phylum in animals is called ______.
questions.e: Plant classes are grouped into divisions.

questions.q: The housefly is Musca domestica. To which genus does it belong?
questions.e: The first word of a scientific name is the genus; Muscidae is its family and Diptera its order.

questions.q: Humans belong to which family?
questions.e: Man: genus Homo, family Hominidae, order Primata, class Mammalia.

questions.q: The mango is Mangifera indica.
p: (a) To which family does it belong?
Anacardiaceae
(b) To which order does it belong?
Sapindales
questions.e: Mango: genus Mangifera, family Anacardiaceae, order Sapindales, class Dicotyledonae, division Angiospermae.

questions.q: In the five kingdom classification, bacteria belong to kingdom ______.
questions.e: Monera are prokaryotes: bacteria, including cyanobacteria.

questions.q: Which kingdom includes all single-celled eukaryotes?
questions.e: Chrysophytes, dinoflagellates, euglenoids, slime moulds and protozoans are protists.

questions.q: The cell wall of fungi is made of ______.
questions.e: Chitin is a complex polysaccharide.

questions.q: Bread mould (Rhizopus) and Mucor belong to the class ______.
questions.e: Phycomycetes have aseptate, coenocytic mycelium.

questions.q: Mushrooms, bracket fungi and puffballs belong to the class ______.
questions.e: Their sexual spores, basidiospores, are formed on a basidium.

questions.q: Fungi whose sexual stage is not known are called imperfect fungi and are placed in the class ______.
questions.e: When their sexual stage is discovered, they are moved to Ascomycetes or Basidiomycetes.

questions.q: Plasmodium, which causes malaria, is a ______ protozoan.
questions.e: Sporozoans have an infectious spore-like stage in their life cycle.

questions.q: Blue-green algae are also called ______.
questions.e: They are photosynthetic bacteria; Nostoc and Anabaena can also fix nitrogen.

questions.q: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) contains which genetic material?
questions.e: Plant viruses generally have single-stranded RNA.

questions.q: A symbiotic association between an alga and a fungus is called a ______.
questions.e: The alga makes food; the fungus provides shelter and absorbs water and minerals.

questions.q: Viruses are non-cellular organisms.
p: (a) What is the protein coat of a virus called?
capsid
(b) What are viruses that infect bacteria called?
bacteriophages|bacteriophage|phages|phage
questions.e: The capsid, made of capsomeres, protects the nucleic acid; bacteriophages usually have double-stranded DNA.

questions.q: Brown algae belong to the class ______.
questions.e: Their colour comes from the pigment fucoxanthin.

questions.q: Plants whose ovules are not enclosed in an ovary, so their seeds are naked, are called ______.
questions.e: Pinus, Cycas and Ginkgo are gymnosperms.

questions.q: Bryophytes are called the ______ of the plant kingdom because they live on land but need water for sexual reproduction.
questions.e: Mosses and liverworts grow in damp, shaded places.

questions.q: The first land plants to have vascular tissues (xylem and phloem) are the ______.
questions.e: Ferns, horsetails and Selaginella are pteridophytes.

questions.q: Members of Chlorophyceae, which store food as starch, are commonly called ______ algae.
questions.e: Chlamydomonas, Volvox and Spirogyra are green algae.

questions.q: Red algae store food as ______ starch.
questions.e: Floridean starch is very similar to amylopectin and glycogen.

questions.q: In pteridophytes, the main plant body is the diploid ______.
questions.e: The gametophyte of a pteridophyte is a small, free-living prothallus.

questions.q: Double fertilisation is a feature unique to ______.
questions.e: It gives both the zygote and the triploid primary endosperm nucleus.

questions.q: The moss Sphagnum provides ______, which is used as fuel and as a packing material.
questions.e: Sphagnum can hold a lot of water, which also makes it useful for packing living material.

questions.q: Agar, used to grow microbes, is obtained from Gelidium and Gracilaria, which are ______ algae.
questions.e: Agar is also used in ice creams and jellies.

questions.q: Angiosperms show double fertilisation.
p: (a) One male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form the ______.
zygote
(b) The other male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the primary ______ nucleus.
endosperm
(c) What is the ploidy of that nucleus? Give the number of chromosome sets.
questions.e: Syngamy forms the diploid zygote; triple fusion forms the triploid (3n) primary endosperm nucleus.

questions.q: Sponges belong to phylum ______.
questions.e: Sponges have a water canal system and collar cells (choanocytes).

questions.q: Which is the largest phylum of the animal kingdom?
questions.e: About two-thirds of all named species on Earth are arthropods, including insects.

questions.q: Earthworms belong to phylum ______.
questions.e: Annelids have a body divided into segments (metameres).

questions.q: Tapeworms and liver flukes, which have dorsoventrally flattened bodies, belong to phylum ______.
questions.e: They are flatworms; most are endoparasites.

questions.q: Animals whose body can be divided into two identical halves along only one plane show ______ symmetry.
questions.e: Annelids, arthropods and chordates are bilaterally symmetrical.

questions.q: Animals that develop from three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm) are called ______.
questions.e: Platyhelminthes to Chordata are triploblastic; sponges and cnidarians are not.

questions.q: Eight external rows of ciliated comb plates, used for swimming, are found in phylum ______.
questions.e: Ctenophores (comb jellies) also show bioluminescence.

questions.q: Birds belong to class ______.
questions.e: Birds have feathers, a beak and forelimbs modified into wings.

questions.q: Sharks have an endoskeleton made of cartilage. To which class do they belong?
questions.e: Bony fishes belong to Osteichthyes.

questions.q: In insects such as the cockroach, excretion takes place through ______ tubules.
questions.e: Malpighian tubules remove nitrogenous wastes from the haemolymph.

questions.q: Members of phylum Mollusca have a soft body.
p: (a) The soft, spongy layer of skin over the visceral hump is called the ______.
mantle
(b) The rasping, file-like feeding organ in the mouth is called the ______.
radula
questions.e: The mantle often secretes a calcareous shell; the radula scrapes food.

questions.q: The main root that develops directly from the radicle is called the ______ root.
questions.e: Dicots such as mustard have a tap root system.

questions.q: Roots that grow from parts of the plant other than the radicle are called ______ roots.
questions.e: Grass, Monstera and the banyan tree have adventitious roots.

questions.q: The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is called ______.
questions.e: Inflorescences are racemose or cymose.

questions.q: The pattern of arrangement of leaves on a stem or branch is called ______.
questions.e: Phyllotaxy can be alternate, opposite or whorled.

questions.q: The banyan tree has hanging roots that grow down from its branches and support them. These are called ______ roots.
questions.e: Stilt roots, as in maize and sugarcane, grow from the lower nodes of the stem.

questions.q: Leaves of monocots generally show ______ venation.
questions.e: Dicot leaves usually have reticulate venation.

questions.q: In potato, the underground stem is modified into a ______ for storing food.
questions.e: The "eyes" of a potato are nodes, which shows that a tuber is a stem.

questions.q: The thorns of Bougainvillea and Citrus are modified ______.
questions.e: Stem thorns grow from axillary buds and protect the plant from browsing animals.

questions.q: A flower that has both androecium and gynoecium is called ______.
questions.e: A flower with only stamens or only carpels is unisexual.

questions.q: A flower in which the ovary is above the other floral parts (a superior ovary) is called ______.
questions.e: Mustard, China rose and brinjal have hypogynous flowers.

questions.q: The fruit of mango is a ______.
questions.e: A drupe develops from a monocarpellary superior ovary and has a hard, stony endocarp.

questions.q: The spines of cacti are modified ______.
questions.e: Spines reduce water loss; the green, fleshy stem carries out photosynthesis.

questions.q: Answer these about the family Solanaceae.
p: (a) Name one vegetable from this family.
potato|tomato|brinjal|chilli|chili|capsicum
(b) What is the placentation?
axile
(c) How many stamens does the flower have?
questions.e: Solanaceae (potato family) has five epipetalous stamens and a bicarpellary, syncarpous ovary with axile placentation.

questions.q: The organelle that is the site of aerobic respiration and produces most of the cell's ATP is the ______.
questions.e: Mitochondria are called the powerhouses of the cell.

questions.q: Cells that have no membrane-bound nucleus are called ______ cells.
questions.e: Bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma and PPLO are prokaryotes.

questions.q: Ribosomes in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells are of the ______ type.
questions.e: Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S; S stands for the Svedberg unit, a measure of sedimentation.

questions.q: The fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane was proposed by Singer and ______.
questions.e: The quasi-fluid lipid bilayer lets proteins move sideways within the membrane.

questions.q: The infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane are called ______.
questions.e: Cristae increase the surface area for respiration.

questions.q: Stacks of thylakoids in a chloroplast are called ______.
questions.e: The grana carry the chlorophyll pigments.

questions.q: The membrane around the vacuole of a plant cell is called the ______.
questions.e: The tonoplast actively moves ions into the vacuole.

questions.q: Endoplasmic reticulum without ribosomes, which makes lipids, is called ______ ER.
questions.e: In animal cells, steroid hormones are made on smooth ER.

questions.q: Which organelles form the basal bodies of cilia and flagella, and the spindle apparatus in animal cells?
questions.e: Centrioles have a cartwheel-like arrangement of nine peripheral triplets of tubulin.

questions.q: The site of active ribosomal RNA synthesis in the nucleus is the ______.
questions.e: Cells that make a lot of protein have larger and more numerous nucleoli.

questions.q: The core of a cilium or flagellum is called the axoneme.
p: (a) How many pairs (doublets) of peripheral microtubules does it have?
(b) How many central microtubules does it have?
questions.e: The axoneme shows the 9 + 2 arrangement: nine peripheral doublets around two central singlet microtubules.

questions.q: A cell division in which the chromosome number is halved is called ______.
questions.e: Meiosis forms haploid gametes; mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same.

questions.q: The division of the cytoplasm after the nucleus has divided is called ______.
questions.e: Karyokinesis is the division of the nucleus.

questions.q: In which phase of interphase is DNA replicated?
questions.e: The amount of DNA doubles in the S phase, but the number of chromosomes stays the same.

questions.q: In mitosis, chromosomes condense and become visible during ______.
questions.e: Prophase follows the S and G2 phases of interphase.

questions.q: In mitosis, the sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles during ______.
questions.e: The centromeres split and each chromatid becomes a daughter chromosome.

questions.q: The pairing of homologous chromosomes during zygotene is called ______.
questions.e: Synapsis is helped by the synaptonemal complex.

questions.q: In plant cells, cytokinesis takes place by the formation of a ______ between the two daughter nuclei.
questions.e: Animal cells divide by a furrow in the plasma membrane instead.

questions.q: Cells that stop dividing leave the G1 phase and enter an inactive stage called ______.
questions.e: Cells in G0 stay metabolically active but do not divide unless needed.

questions.q: The X-shaped points where crossing over has taken place, seen during diplotene, are called ______.
questions.e: The homologous chromosomes stay joined at the chiasmata as they start to separate.

questions.q: A typical human cell growing in culture divides about once in how many hours?
questions.e: Of this, the M phase lasts only about an hour; the rest is interphase.

questions.q: A plant cell has 16 chromosomes.
p: (a) How many chromosomes does each daughter cell have after mitosis?
(b) How many chromosomes does each cell have at the end of meiosis II?
questions.e: Mitosis keeps the number the same; meiosis I halves it to 8, and meiosis II (like mitosis) keeps it at 8.

questions.q: The light reactions of photosynthesis take place in the ______ of the chloroplast.
questions.e: The pigments and electron carriers are in the thylakoid membranes.

questions.q: The Calvin cycle (the biosynthetic phase) takes place in the ______ of the chloroplast.
questions.e: The enzymes of the Calvin cycle, including RuBisCO, are in the stroma.

questions.q: The oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from ______.
questions.e: Water is split in the light reaction, releasing oxygen, protons and electrons.

questions.q: The reaction centre of Photosystem I is a chlorophyll a molecule with an absorption peak at ______ nm.
questions.e: It is called P700; the reaction centre of Photosystem II is P680.

questions.q: The splitting of water during the light reaction is called ______.
questions.e: It is linked to Photosystem II.

questions.q: The synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using light energy is called ______.
questions.e: It takes place by chemiosmosis across the thylakoid membrane.

questions.q: In C4 plants, the first stable product of CO2 fixation is the 4-carbon ______.
questions.e: PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 in the mesophyll cells to form oxaloacetic acid.

questions.q: Besides absorbing extra light, accessory pigments such as carotenoids protect chlorophyll a from ______.
questions.e: They also widen the range of wavelengths used for photosynthesis.

questions.q: How many molecules of CO2 must be fixed in the Calvin cycle to make one molecule of glucose?
questions.e: Glucose has six carbon atoms, so six turns of the cycle are needed.

questions.q: The wasteful process in C3 plants in which RuBisCO binds oxygen instead of CO2 is called ______.
questions.e: Photorespiration makes neither sugar nor ATP; C4 plants avoid it.

questions.q: Consider the making of one molecule of glucose in the Calvin cycle.
p: (a) How many molecules of NADPH are used?
(b) How many turns of the cycle are needed?
questions.e: Each turn fixes one CO2 and uses 3 ATP and 2 NADPH, so six turns use 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.

questions.q: Glycolysis breaks one molecule of glucose into two molecules of ______.
questions.e: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm of all living organisms.

questions.q: The Krebs cycle takes place in the ______ of the mitochondria.
questions.e: The electron transport system is on the inner mitochondrial membrane.

questions.q: Respiration that takes place without oxygen is called ______ respiration.
questions.e: Fermentation by yeast is an example.

questions.q: Glycolysis is also called the EMP pathway, after Embden, Meyerhof and ______.
questions.e: It was worked out by these three scientists.

questions.q: The Krebs cycle is also called the ______ cycle.
questions.e: It begins when acetyl CoA combines with oxaloacetic acid to form citric acid.

questions.q: In mitochondria, ATP is made from ADP and phosphate by the enzyme ATP ______.
questions.e: ATP synthase (complex V) uses the flow of protons back across the inner membrane.

questions.q: What is the net gain of ATP molecules directly from glycolysis of one glucose molecule?
questions.e: Four ATP are made but two are used, giving a net gain of 2 (plus 2 NADH).

questions.q: What is the approximate respiratory quotient (RQ) when proteins are used as the respiratory substrate?
questions.e: RQ is about 1 for carbohydrates, 0.7 for fats and 0.9 for proteins.

questions.q: In the mitochondria, pyruvic acid is converted into ______ before it enters the Krebs cycle.
questions.e: This oxidative decarboxylation also releases CO2 and forms NADH.

questions.q: According to NCERT, how many ATP molecules are made from one molecule of NADH through oxidative phosphorylation?
questions.e: One FADH2 gives 2 ATP.

questions.q: The respiratory pathway is called amphibolic because it is involved in both catabolism and ______.
questions.e: Its intermediates are also used to make fatty acids and amino acids.

questions.q: Consider the complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule, as given in NCERT.
p: (a) What is the net gain of ATP?
(b) How many ATP molecules does one FADH2 give?
questions.e: NCERT gives a net gain of 38 ATP per glucose in aerobic respiration, with each NADH giving 3 ATP and each FADH2 giving 2 ATP.

questions.q: The thin-walled air sacs in the lungs, where gases are exchanged, are called ______.
questions.e: Alveoli give a very large, thin, moist surface surrounded by capillaries.

questions.q: The dome-shaped muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity is the ______.
questions.e: The diaphragm contracts during inspiration, increasing the volume of the chest.

questions.q: The double-layered membrane that covers the lungs is the ______.
questions.e: Pleural fluid between the layers reduces friction on the lung surface.

questions.q: About 97% of the oxygen in blood is carried by red blood cells as ______.
questions.e: The remaining 3% is dissolved in the plasma.

questions.q: About 70% of the carbon dioxide in blood is carried as ______.
questions.e: About 20–25% is carried as carbaminohaemoglobin and about 7% dissolved in plasma.

questions.q: The enzyme in red blood cells that speeds up the reaction of carbon dioxide with water to form carbonic acid is ______.
questions.e: The same enzyme works in reverse in the lungs to release CO2.

questions.q: The respiratory rhythm centre is in the ______ region of the brain.
questions.e: The pneumotaxic centre in the pons can modify it.

questions.q: What is the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli, in mm Hg?
questions.e: It is 104 mm Hg in the alveoli and 40 mm Hg in deoxygenated blood, so oxygen diffuses into the blood.

questions.q: The volume of air that remains in the lungs even after a forcible expiration is called the ______ volume.
questions.e: It is about 1100–1200 mL.

questions.q: Difficulty in breathing with wheezing, caused by inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles, is called ______.
questions.e: Asthma is often triggered by allergies.

questions.q: A chronic disorder in which the alveolar walls are damaged, reducing the surface for gas exchange, is called ______. Smoking is a major cause.
questions.e: The damaged alveoli lose their elasticity.

questions.q: A person breathes 12 times a minute with a tidal volume of 500 mL.
p: (a) How much air does the person breathe in per minute?
mL
(b) How much is that per hour, in litres?
L
questions.e: 500 × 12 = 6000 mL per minute; 6 L × 60 = 360 L per hour.

questions.q: The straw-coloured fluid part of blood is called ______.
questions.e: Plasma is about 55% of blood; 90–92% of it is water.

questions.q: Red blood cells are also called ______.
questions.e: They are the most abundant cells in blood and carry haemoglobin.

questions.q: Platelets (thrombocytes) help in the ______ of blood.
questions.e: A fall in platelet count can lead to excessive loss of blood from a wound.

questions.q: Human red blood cells have an average lifespan of about ______ days.
questions.e: Old RBCs are destroyed in the spleen, the graveyard of RBCs.

questions.q: The most abundant white blood cells are the ______.
questions.e: Neutrophils are about 60–65% of white cells and destroy microbes by phagocytosis.

questions.q: The valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle is the ______ valve.
questions.e: It has three flaps; the bicuspid (mitral) valve is on the left side.

questions.q: Blood that has antigen B on its red cells and anti-A antibodies in its plasma belongs to blood group ______.
questions.e: Group A has antigen A and anti-B; group AB has both antigens and no antibodies.

questions.q: The first heart sound, "lub", is caused by the closure of the ______ valves.
questions.e: The second sound, "dub", comes from the closure of the semilunar valves.

questions.q: If the heart beats 75 times a minute, how long does one cardiac cycle last?
A condition in which deposits of calcium, fat and fibrous tissue narrow the coronary arteries is called coronary artery disease, or ______.
questions.e: It reduces the blood supply to the heart muscle.

questions.q: In an ECG, the QRS complex represents the ______ of the ventricles.
questions.e: The P wave is atrial depolarisation and the T wave is ventricular repolarisation.

questions.q: A healthy adult has a blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg.
p: (a) What is the systolic pressure?
mm Hg
(b) What is the diastolic pressure?
mm Hg
(c) A pressure of 140/90 or higher, again and again, is called ______.
hypertension|high blood pressure
questions.e: Systolic is the pumping pressure and diastolic the resting pressure. Hypertension can lead to heart disease and affect the brain and kidneys.

questions.q: The common Indian frog is Rana ______.
questions.e: Frogs are amphibians.

questions.q: Frogs are cold-blooded: their body temperature changes with the surroundings. Such animals are called ______.
questions.e: Birds and mammals, which keep a constant body temperature, are homeotherms.

questions.q: Frogs escape the heat of summer by staying in burrows. This summer sleep is called ______.
questions.e: Winter sleep is called hibernation.

questions.q: Epithelium made of a single thin layer of flattened cells with irregular boundaries is called squamous, or ______, epithelium.
questions.e: It lines the walls of blood vessels and the air sacs of the lungs.

questions.q: Cells in neural tissue that support and protect the neurons are called ______ cells.
questions.e: Neuroglia make up more than half the volume of neural tissue in our body.

questions.q: The loose connective tissue specialised to store fat is ______ tissue.
questions.e: It lies mainly beneath the skin.

questions.q: Almost all enzymes are ______.
questions.e: Some nucleic acids (ribozymes) also act as enzymes.

questions.q: The monomer units of nucleic acids are called ______.
questions.e: A nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group.

questions.q: In DNA, adenine always pairs with ______.
questions.e: Guanine pairs with cytosine.

questions.q: Cellulose is a polymer of ______.
questions.e: Cellulose is a homopolymer of glucose and forms plant cell walls.

questions.q: A non-protein organic group tightly bound to an enzyme, such as haem in peroxidase, is called a ______ group.
questions.e: Coenzymes, by contrast, bind to the enzyme only during the reaction.

questions.q: Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering their ______ energy.
questions.e: The substrate needs less energy to reach the transition state.

questions.q: Auxin was first isolated from human ______.
questions.e: Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) is the main natural auxin.

questions.q: Which group of plant growth regulators is widely used to make stem cuttings form roots?
questions.e: Auxins such as IBA and NAA promote rooting.

questions.q: Which group of plant growth regulators delays leaf senescence (ageing)?
questions.e: Cytokinins help produce new leaves and chloroplasts and delay ageing.

questions.q: Growth in which both daughter cells keep dividing, giving an exponential increase, is called ______ growth.
questions.e: When nutrients run short, geometric growth slows down and gives an S-shaped curve.

questions.q: The sigmoid growth curve has a lag phase, a log (exponential) phase and a ______ phase.
questions.e: Growth slows and stops in the stationary phase as resources become limited.

questions.q: Which plant growth regulator causes the stomata to close when a plant is short of water?
questions.e: ABA increases the plant's tolerance to stress.

questions.q: Animals such as bony fishes, which excrete mainly ammonia, are called ______.
questions.e: Ammonia is very toxic and needs a lot of water to remove it.

questions.q: In mammals, urea is made in the ______.
questions.e: Ammonia is turned into urea in the liver and removed by the kidneys.

questions.q: The process of passing out urine is called ______.
questions.e: It is controlled by a neural reflex.

questions.q: The excretory structures of earthworms are called ______.
questions.e: Flame cells are found in flatworms and Malpighian tubules in insects.

questions.q: Nearly what percentage of the glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed by the renal tubules?
questions.e: Of 180 L of filtrate a day, only about 1.5 L leaves as urine.

questions.q: The presence of glucose in urine is called ______.
questions.e: Glycosuria, with ketone bodies in urine (ketonuria), points to diabetes mellitus.

questions.q: Muscle fibres contain the contractile proteins actin and ______.
questions.e: Thin filaments are actin; thick filaments are myosin.

questions.q: The knee joint is a ______ joint.
questions.e: Hinge joints allow movement in one plane, like a door.

questions.q: The joint between the humerus and the pectoral girdle (the shoulder) is a ______ joint.
questions.e: It allows movement in many directions.

questions.q: Inflammation of the joints caused by the build-up of uric acid crystals is called ______.
questions.e: Osteoporosis is the loss of bone mass with age.

questions.q: How many bones are there in each human limb (one arm or one leg)?
questions.e: Each of the four limbs has 30 bones.

questions.q: Muscle contraction is explained by the ______ theory, in which the thin filaments slide over the thick filaments.
questions.e: The sarcomere shortens as actin slides over myosin; the A band keeps its length.

questions.q: The largest part of the human brain is the ______.
questions.e: The cerebrum has two cerebral hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum.

questions.q: The brain is protected by three layers of membranes called the ______.
questions.e: They are the dura mater, arachnoid and pia mater.

questions.q: The autonomic nervous system has two divisions: the sympathetic and the ______ nervous system.
questions.e: It controls involuntary organs and smooth muscles.

questions.q: Chemicals released at a chemical synapse that carry the impulse to the next neuron are called ______.
questions.e: They bind to receptors on the post-synaptic membrane.

questions.q: In a reflex arc, the neuron that carries impulses from the receptor to the spinal cord is the ______ neuron.
questions.e: The efferent (motor) neuron carries the signal from the spinal cord to the effector.

questions.q: At rest, the outer surface of the axonal membrane is ______ charged relative to the inner surface.
questions.e: The membrane is polarised; the resting potential is due to the uneven distribution of ions.

questions.q: Which endocrine gland, attached to the hypothalamus, controls many other endocrine glands?
questions.e: The pituitary is divided into the adenohypophysis and the neurohypophysis.

questions.q: Oxytocin stimulates strong contractions of the uterus during childbirth. These are ______ muscles.
questions.e: Oxytocin also causes milk ejection from the mammary glands.

questions.q: Too much growth hormone in adults, especially in middle age, causes ______.
questions.e: Too much growth hormone in childhood causes gigantism.

questions.q: Hypothyroidism during pregnancy causes defective development of the baby, leading to ______.
questions.e: It causes stunted growth and mental retardation.

questions.q: Glucagon raises the level of glucose in the blood, so it is a ______ hormone.
questions.e: Insulin, which lowers blood glucose, is a hypoglycemic hormone.

questions.q: Testosterone is produced by the ______ cells in the testes.
questions.e: Leydig cells lie in the spaces between the seminiferous tubules.

questions.q: The part of the pistil that serves as the landing platform for pollen grains is the ______.
questions.e: Each pistil has a stigma, a style and an ovary; pollen grains land on the stigma.

questions.q: Pollination by wind is called ______.
questions.e: Wind-pollinated flowers produce light, non-sticky pollen in large numbers and often have feathery stigmas.

questions.q: The stalk by which an ovule is attached to the placenta is called the ______.
questions.e: The funicle joins the body of the ovule at the hilum.

questions.q: Transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower is called ______.
questions.e: In autogamy pollination is achieved within the same flower.

questions.q: Transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of another flower of the same plant is called ______.
questions.e: Geitonogamy is functionally cross-pollination but genetically similar to autogamy, as the pollen comes from the same plant.

questions.q: Flowers of Viola, Oxalis and Commelina that do not open at all are called ______ flowers.
questions.e: Cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous and produce assured seed set even without pollinators.

questions.q: Some species, such as certain grasses and Asteraceae, produce seeds without fertilisation. This is called ______.
questions.e: Apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction.

questions.q: The occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed, as in many Citrus and mango varieties, is called ______.
questions.e: Some nucellar cells divide and protrude into the embryo sac to form extra embryos, giving polyembryony.

questions.q: In over 60 per cent of angiosperms, pollen grains are shed at the ______-celled stage.
questions.e: At this stage the pollen grain contains a vegetative cell and a generative cell; in the rest, the generative cell divides first to give the 3-celled stage.

questions.q: In seeds of black pepper and beet, the residual, persistent nucellus is called the ______.
questions.e: Usually the nucellus is used up, but in black pepper and beet some of it persists as perisperm.

questions.q: Answer the following about the embryo of grasses (monocots).
p: (a) What is the single cotyledon called?
scutellum
(b) What is the sheath enclosing the shoot apex and leaf primordia called?
coleoptile
(c) What is the sheath enclosing the radicle and root cap called?
coleorhiza
questions.e: A grass embryo has one large, shield-shaped cotyledon, the scutellum; the epicotyl is covered by the coleoptile and the radicle by the coleorhiza.

questions.q: The release of the ovum from the Graafian follicle is called ______.
questions.e: Ovulation normally takes place around the middle (about the 14th day) of the menstrual cycle.

questions.q: The first menstruation, which begins at puberty, is called ______.
