questions.e: Menarche marks the start of the menstrual cycles; menopause (around 50 years) marks their end.

questions.q: The embedding of the blastocyst in the endometrium of the uterus is called ______.
questions.e: The trophoblast layer attaches to the endometrium and the blastocyst becomes embedded in it; implantation leads to pregnancy.

questions.q: A rapid surge of which pituitary hormone in the middle of the menstrual cycle induces ovulation?
questions.e: The LH surge induces rupture of the Graafian follicle and the release of the ovum.

questions.q: After ovulation, the remaining parts of the Graafian follicle transform into a structure that secretes large amounts of progesterone. It is called the ______.
questions.e: Progesterone from the corpus luteum maintains the endometrium; without fertilisation the corpus luteum degenerates and menstruation follows.

questions.q: Each testis has about how many compartments called testicular lobules?
questions.e: Each of the about 250 testicular lobules contains one to three highly coiled seminiferous tubules.

questions.q: The release of sperms from the seminiferous tubules is called ______.
questions.e: Sperm heads are embedded in Sertoli cells and are finally released from the seminiferous tubules by spermiation.

questions.q: The transformation of spermatids into spermatozoa (sperms) is called ______.
questions.e: Spermiogenesis is the change of the round spermatids into tailed sperms; spermiation is their later release.

questions.q: Signals from the fully developed foetus and placenta trigger the release of a hormone from the mother's pituitary that causes stronger uterine contractions during parturition. Name the hormone.
questions.e: Oxytocin acts on the uterine muscle; the stronger contractions stimulate further oxytocin secretion (foetal ejection reflex).

questions.q: The outer layer of cells of the blastocyst, which gets attached to the endometrium, is called the ______.
questions.e: The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium, while the inner cell mass differentiates into the embryo.

questions.q: How many ova will be formed from 10 primary oocytes?
questions.e: Each primary oocyte gives one ovum; the other products of the unequal meiotic divisions are polar bodies.

questions.q: Answer the following about spermatogenesis in human males.
p: (a) How many chromosomes does a primary spermatocyte have?
(b) How many chromosomes does a spermatid have?
(c) Which hypothalamic hormone, whose increased secretion at puberty starts spermatogenesis, acts on the pituitary to release LH and FSH?
GnRH|gonadotropin releasing hormone|gonadotrophin releasing hormone
questions.e: Primary spermatocytes are diploid (46); meiosis gives haploid spermatids (23); GnRH from the hypothalamus increases LH and FSH secretion.

questions.q: The surgical method of contraception in males, in which a small part of the vas deferens is removed or tied up, is called ______.
questions.e: Vasectomy blocks the transport of sperms; it is a terminal (permanent) method.

questions.q: The surgical method of contraception in females, in which a small part of the fallopian tube is removed or tied up, is called ______.
questions.e: Tubectomy blocks the transport of the ovum; reversibility is very poor.

questions.q: 'Nirodh' is a popular brand of ______ for males in India.
questions.e: Condoms are barriers made of thin rubber or latex that prevent sperms from reaching the female reproductive tract and also protect against STIs.

questions.q: The once-a-week oral contraceptive pill 'Saheli' was developed by scientists at which institute in Lucknow?
questions.e: Saheli, a non-steroidal pill with very few side effects and high contraceptive value, was developed at CDRI, Lucknow.

questions.q: The natural method in which couples avoid coitus from day 10 to 17 of the menstrual cycle, when ovulation is expected, is called ______.
questions.e: Chances of fertilisation are very high during this fertile period, so avoiding coitus then can prevent conception.

questions.q: Lactational amenorrhoea is effective as a contraceptive method only up to a maximum of how many months following parturition?
questions.e: Ovulation and menstruation do not occur during intense lactation, but this method has been reported to be effective only up to six months after parturition.

questions.q: Medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) is considered relatively safe during the first trimester, that is, up to how many weeks of pregnancy?
questions.e: MTPs are relatively safe up to 12 weeks; second-trimester abortions are much riskier.

questions.q: Progestogens, alone or with oestrogens, can be used by females as injections or as ______ placed under the skin.
questions.e: Hormonal injections and implants work like pills, but their effective periods are much longer.

questions.q: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act was enacted by the Government of India in which year?
questions.e: The MTP (Amendment) Act, 2017 was enacted to reduce maternal deaths from unsafe abortions; it lays down when and by whom a pregnancy may be terminated.

questions.q: In GIFT, what is transferred into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce one but can provide suitable conditions for fertilisation?
questions.e: GIFT is gamete intra fallopian transfer: an ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube.

questions.q: The specialised procedure in which a sperm is directly injected into the ovum to form an embryo in the laboratory is called ______.
questions.a: ICSI|intracytoplasmic sperm injection|intra cytoplasmic sperm injection
questions.e: ICSI is intracytoplasmic sperm injection, one of the assisted reproductive technologies.

questions.q: Infertility due to a male partner's inability to inseminate or very low sperm count can be corrected by introducing semen into the uterus. This is called ______.
questions.e: In artificial insemination the semen is introduced into the vagina or into the uterus (IUI, intra-uterine insemination).

questions.q: Answer the following about reproductive health in India.
p: (a) What were India's national reproductive health programmes, started in 1951, called?
family planning
(b) LNG-20 is an example of which type of IUD: copper releasing or hormone releasing?
hormone releasing|hormone|hormone-releasing
(c) Within how many hours of coitus must emergency contraceptives (pills or IUDs) be used?
hours
questions.e: India's 'family planning' programmes began in 1951; Progestasert and LNG-20 are hormone-releasing IUDs; emergency contraception works if used within 72 hours of coitus.

questions.q: The units of inheritance that Mendel called 'factors' are now called ______.
questions.e: Factors are now called genes; genes that code for a pair of contrasting traits are alleles.

questions.q: Crossing an organism showing the dominant phenotype with its recessive parent, to find its genotype, is called a ______.
questions.e: In a test cross the progeny reveal whether the dominant-looking organism is homozygous or heterozygous.

questions.q: Down's syndrome is caused by an additional copy of chromosome number ______.
questions.e: Trisomy of chromosome 21 causes Down's syndrome; affected individuals are short with a small round head and furrowed tongue.

questions.q: In humans, the ABO blood groups are controlled by the gene I, which has how many alleles?
questions.e: The three alleles are IA, IB and i; this is an example of multiple alleles.

questions.q: When a single gene shows multiple phenotypic expressions, as in phenylketonuria, the gene is called a ______ gene.
questions.e: A pleiotropic gene affects many traits; in phenylketonuria, a single gene mutation causes mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation.

questions.q: Human skin colour, controlled by three or more genes with additive effects, is an example of ______ inheritance.
questions.e: In polygenic inheritance each allele adds its effect, and the trait shows a continuous range of phenotypes.

questions.q: In sickle-cell anaemia, glutamic acid at the sixth position of the beta-globin chain of haemoglobin is replaced by ______.
questions.e: The single base substitution changes the codon GAG to GUG, so valine replaces glutamic acid.

questions.q: How many different genotypes are possible for the human ABO blood groups?
questions.e: Three alleles give 6 genotypes (IAIA, IAi, IBIB, IBi, IAIB, ii) but only 4 phenotypes.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are present in the body cells of a person with Turner's syndrome?
questions.e: Turner's syndrome is caused by the absence of one X chromosome (45 with XO); Klinefelter's syndrome has 47 (XXY).

questions.q: The scientist who worked on Drosophila and coined the term 'linkage' for the physical association of genes on a chromosome was ______.
questions.a: Thomas Hunt Morgan|Morgan|T. H. Morgan|T H Morgan|Thomas Morgan
questions.e: Morgan found that some gene combinations stayed together more often than expected and called this linkage; non-parental combinations he called recombination.

questions.q: A pea plant heterozygous for two independently assorting genes (RrYy) is crossed with a double recessive plant (rryy).
p: (a) How many phenotypic classes appear among the progeny?
(b) What percentage of the progeny are expected to be rryy?
(c) Which of Mendel's laws explains these results?
law of independent assortment|independent assortment
questions.e: RrYy gives four kinds of gametes (RY, Ry, rY, ry) in equal numbers, so the test cross gives four classes in a 1:1:1:1 ratio, each 25%.

questions.q: The process of copying genetic information from one strand of DNA into RNA is called ______.
questions.e: Transcription produces RNA; translation then uses mRNA to make a polypeptide.

questions.q: In bacteria, a single DNA-dependent ______ catalyses the transcription of all types of RNA.
questions.e: Bacteria have one RNA polymerase; eukaryotes have three (I, II and III) in the nucleus.

questions.q: How many nucleotides make up one codon of the genetic code?
questions.e: The code is a triplet: three nucleotides code for one amino acid.

questions.q: Frederick Griffith's transformation experiments (1928) were done with the bacterium Streptococcus ______.
questions.e: Heat-killed S strain bacteria transformed live R strain bacteria into the virulent S form in mice.

questions.q: Hershey and Chase grew bacteriophages on a medium containing radioactive ______ to label their DNA.
questions.e: DNA contains phosphorus but not sulphur; proteins were labelled with 35S. Only 32P entered the bacteria, showing that DNA is the genetic material.

questions.q: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty found that the transforming principle of Griffith was destroyed only by the enzyme ______.
questions.e: Proteases and RNases did not affect transformation, but DNase stopped it, so the transforming substance was DNA.

questions.q: In bacteria, RNA polymerase associates transiently with the ______ factor to initiate transcription.
questions.e: The sigma factor helps initiation; the rho factor helps termination.

questions.q: Which RNA acts as an adapter molecule that reads the code on one side and binds a specific amino acid on the other?
questions.e: tRNA has an anticodon loop that pairs with the codon and an amino acid acceptor end.

questions.q: In eukaryotes, the intervening sequences that do not appear in mature mRNA and are removed by splicing are called ______.
questions.e: In the primary transcript (hnRNA), introns are removed and exons are joined in a defined order.

questions.q: How many histone molecules make up the histone octamer of a nucleosome?
questions.e: Negatively charged DNA is wrapped around a positively charged histone octamer to form a nucleosome, which contains about 200 bp of DNA.

questions.q: Answer the following about the lac operon of E. coli.
p: (a) Which enzyme is coded by the z gene?
beta-galactosidase|beta galactosidase|β-galactosidase
(b) Is the regulation of the lac operon by the repressor positive or negative?
negative
(c) How many structural genes does the lac operon have?
questions.e: The z, y and a genes code for beta-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase; the repressor switches the operon off, so this is negative regulation.

questions.q: The Earth was formed about how many billion years ago?
questions.e: The universe is about 20 billion years old; the Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago.

questions.q: Hugo de Vries, working on the evening primrose, proposed that evolution is caused by ______, not by minor variations.
questions.e: de Vries believed large mutations cause speciation in a single step, which he called saltation.

questions.q: The idea that the long neck of the giraffe evolved because ancestors kept stretching their necks to reach leaves (use and disuse of organs) was given by ______.
questions.e: Lamarck proposed that characters acquired through use and disuse are inherited; this view is no longer accepted.

questions.q: The evolution of different varieties of finches from a seed-eating ancestor on the Galapagos Islands is an example of ______ radiation.
questions.e: Darwin's finches show adaptive radiation: evolution of different forms starting from one point and radiating to other habitats.

questions.q: Oparin of Russia and ______ of England proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules.
questions.a: Haldane|J. B. S. Haldane|J B S Haldane
questions.e: They suggested that the formation of life was preceded by chemical evolution.

questions.q: In S.L. Miller's experiment, an electric discharge in a closed flask containing CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 800 °C produced ______.
questions.e: Miller observed the formation of amino acids; others in similar experiments observed sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments and fats.

questions.q: When more than one adaptive radiation occurs in an isolated geographical area, as with Australian marsupials and placental mammals, it is called ______ evolution.
questions.e: Marsupials and placental mammals in Australia evolved similar forms in similar habitats, such as the marsupial mole and the placental mole.

questions.q: The first human-like being, the hominid, with a brain capacity of 650-800 cc, was called ______.
questions.e: Homo habilis probably did not eat meat; Homo erectus, with a brain of about 900 cc, came later.

questions.q: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 16% of individuals show the recessive phenotype (aa). What is the frequency of the dominant allele (p)?

When a small group that moves away from a population has allele frequencies so different that it becomes a new species, the original drifted population becomes the founders. This is called the ______ effect.
questions.e: The founder effect is a consequence of genetic drift, a change in allele frequency by chance.

questions.q: Alfred Wallace, a naturalist who came to conclusions similar to those of Darwin, worked in which archipelago?
questions.e: Wallace, working in the Malay Archipelago, reached conclusions about natural selection similar to Darwin's.

questions.q: State whether each pair of organs is homologous or analogous.
p: (a) Thorns of Bougainvillea and tendrils of Cucurbita
homologous
(b) Eye of the octopus and eye of mammals
analogous
(c) Sweet potato (a root) and potato (a stem)
analogous
questions.e: Thorns and tendrils are both modified stems (divergent evolution); the eyes and the storage organs have similar functions but different origins (convergent evolution).

questions.q: Pneumonia in humans is caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and ______ influenzae.
questions.e: These bacteria infect the alveoli of the lungs, which fill with fluid, causing problems in breathing.

questions.q: Amoebic dysentery (amoebiasis) is caused by the protozoan Entamoeba ______.
questions.e: Entamoeba histolytica lives in the large intestine; houseflies act as mechanical carriers.

questions.q: The common cold is caused by a group of viruses called ______.
questions.e: Rhino viruses infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs.

questions.q: Elephantiasis (filariasis) is caused by filarial worms of the genus ______.
questions.e: Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi are transmitted by female mosquito vectors and cause chronic inflammation of the lymphatic vessels.

questions.q: Ringworm is caused by fungi of the genera Microsporum, Trichophyton and ______.
questions.e: These fungi cause dry, scaly lesions on the skin, nails and scalp; heat and moisture help them grow.

questions.q: The army of proteins called antibodies is produced in response to pathogens by which type of lymphocytes?
questions.e: B-lymphocytes produce antibodies (humoral immunity); T-cells help B-cells and mediate cell-mediated immunity.

questions.q: A widely used diagnostic test for AIDS is ______.
questions.a: ELISA|enzyme linked immunosorbent assay|enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
questions.e: ELISA (enzyme linked immunosorbent assay) detects HIV antibodies; the Widal test is for typhoid.

questions.q: Allergic reactions involve release of histamine and serotonin from mast cells and are caused by antibodies of type ______.
questions.e: Allergens trigger IgE antibodies; anti-histamines, adrenalin and steroids reduce the symptoms.

questions.q: After infecting a cell, HIV makes a DNA copy of its RNA genome using the enzyme ______.
questions.e: HIV is a retrovirus; the viral DNA gets incorporated into the host cell DNA and directs the formation of new virus particles.

questions.q: In malaria, the chill and high fever recurring every three to four days are due to the release of a toxic substance called ______ when RBCs rupture.
questions.e: Plasmodium multiplies in RBCs; their rupture releases haemozoin.

questions.q: Answer the following about the life cycle of Plasmodium.
p: (a) Apart from liver cells, in which human cells does Plasmodium multiply asexually?
RBCs|RBC|red blood cells|erythrocytes|red blood cell
(b) Which stages, developed in the RBCs, are taken up by the female Anopheles mosquito when it bites?
gametocytes|gametocyte
(c) In which organ of the mosquito are the sporozoites stored before being injected into humans?
salivary glands|salivary gland
questions.e: Gametocytes fuse in the mosquito gut and develop into sporozoites, which are stored in the salivary glands and injected with the bite.

questions.q: Toddy, a traditional drink of some parts of southern India, is made by fermenting sap from ______.
questions.e: Microbes ferment palm sap to make toddy.

questions.q: Dough for bread is fermented using baker's yeast, Saccharomyces ______.
questions.e: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is used in bread-making and, as brewer's yeast, in making alcoholic drinks.

questions.q: Penicillin, the first antibiotic to be discovered, was discovered by Alexander ______.
questions.e: Fleming noticed that a mould (Penicillium notatum) growing on Staphylococcus cultures stopped the bacteria from growing.

questions.q: Citric acid is produced commercially by the fungus Aspergillus ______.
questions.e: Aspergillus niger produces citric acid; Acetobacter aceti produces acetic acid.

questions.q: Butyric acid is produced by the bacterium ______ butylicum.
questions.e: Clostridium butylicum makes butyric acid; Lactobacillus makes lactic acid.

questions.q: Streptokinase, produced by the bacterium Streptococcus, is used to remove ______ from the blood vessels of patients who have had a myocardial infarction.
questions.e: Streptokinase, modified by genetic engineering, is used as a 'clot buster'.

questions.q: During secondary treatment of sewage, masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments form mesh-like structures called ______.
questions.e: Aerobic microbes in the flocs consume the organic matter in the effluent, which reduces its BOD.

questions.q: The amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria is called the ______.
questions.e: BOD measures the organic matter in water; the greater the BOD of waste water, the more is its polluting potential.

questions.q: Bacteria such as Methanobacterium, which grow anaerobically on cellulosic material and produce large amounts of methane, are collectively called ______.
questions.e: Methanogens occur in sludge and in the rumen of cattle, and are used to produce biogas.

questions.q: Many members of the fungal genus ______ form mycorrhiza, which absorbs phosphorus from the soil and passes it to the plant.
questions.e: Plants with mycorrhizal associations also show resistance to root-borne pathogens and tolerance to salinity and drought.

questions.q: Baculoviruses used as biological control agents against insects and arthropods mostly belong to the genus ______.
questions.e: Nucleopolyhedroviruses are species-specific, narrow-spectrum insecticides with no negative effects on plants, mammals, birds or non-target insects.

questions.q: Answer the following about microbial products.
p: (a) Lipases are used in which type of product to help remove oily stains from laundry?
detergents|detergent|detergent formulations
(b) Bottled fruit juices are clarified using pectinases and which other enzymes?
proteases|protease
(c) Statins, which lower blood cholesterol, are produced by which yeast?
Monascus purpureus|Monascus
questions.e: Lipases act in detergents, pectinases and proteases make juices clearer, and statins from Monascus purpureus competitively inhibit the enzyme that synthesises cholesterol.

questions.q: The sequence in a vector from where replication starts, which also controls the copy number of the linked DNA, is called ______.
questions.e: Any DNA linked to the ori can be made to replicate in the host cell.

questions.q: In the restriction enzyme EcoRI, the letters 'Eco' come from the name of the bacterium ______.
questions.e: The first letter comes from the genus and the next two from the species; R is the strain RY 13 and I shows it was the first enzyme isolated from it.

questions.q: The enzyme used to join the cut piece of foreign DNA to the cut vector DNA is DNA ______.
questions.e: DNA ligase joins the sticky ends of the insert and the vector to make recombinant DNA.

questions.q: The thermostable DNA polymerase used in PCR is isolated from the bacterium ______.
questions.e: Taq polymerase stays active during the high temperature needed to denature double-stranded DNA.

questions.q: To release DNA, bacterial cells are treated with lysozyme, plant cells with cellulase and fungal cells with ______.
questions.e: Fungal cell walls contain chitin, so chitinase is used to break them.

questions.q: Bacterial cells are made competent to take up DNA by treating them with a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as ______.
questions.e: Calcium increases the efficiency with which DNA enters the bacterium through pores in its cell wall; heat shock then follows.

questions.q: In gel electrophoresis, separated DNA fragments stained with ethidium bromide are seen under UV light as bright ______ coloured bands.
questions.e: Pure DNA cannot be seen in visible light; ethidium bromide staining followed by UV exposure shows the bands.

questions.q: The separated DNA bands are cut out from the agarose gel and extracted from the gel piece. This step is called ______.
questions.e: Purified DNA fragments obtained by elution are used to construct recombinant DNA.

questions.q: According to NCERT, the most commonly used bioreactors are of the ______ type.
questions.e: A stirred-tank bioreactor is usually cylindrical with a curved base to mix the contents, and a stirrer for even mixing and oxygen availability.

questions.q: The processes of separation and purification of the product after biosynthesis, before it is ready for marketing, are collectively called ______.
questions.e: The product is formulated with suitable preservatives and, for drugs, put through clinical trials and quality control.

questions.q: Answer the following about the polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
p: (a) What is the step in which double-stranded DNA is separated by heating called?
denaturation
(b) What is the step in which primers bind to the single strands called?
annealing
(c) Starting with one DNA molecule, how many copies are present after 3 cycles?
questions.e: Each cycle has denaturation, annealing and extension, and doubles the DNA: 1 to 2, 4 and 8 copies after 3 cycles.

questions.q: The Bacillus thuringiensis genes that code for the insecticidal Bt toxin proteins are called ______ genes.
questions.e: The cry genes are named so because they code for crystal (Cry) proteins.

questions.q: Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are called ______ organisms.
questions.e: GM plants can be more tolerant to stresses, less dependent on chemical pesticides and more nutritious.

questions.q: Before recombinant insulin, insulin for diabetic patients was extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and ______.
questions.e: Animal insulin caused allergy or other reactions in some patients, which led to recombinant human insulin.

questions.q: The proteins encoded by the genes cryIAc and cryIIAb control the cotton ______.
questions.e: cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms, while cryIAb controls the corn borer.

questions.q: Bt toxin protein exists in the bacterium as an inactive ______, so it does not kill the bacterium.
questions.e: In the insect gut it is converted into the active toxin, which binds to the midgut epithelial cells and creates pores.

questions.q: The inactive Bt protoxin is converted into the active toxin in the insect gut because of the ______ pH there.
questions.e: The alkaline pH of the gut solubilises the crystals, and the active toxin causes cell swelling and lysis, killing the insect.

questions.q: Insulin is synthesised as a prohormone with an extra stretch called the ______ peptide, which is removed during maturation.
questions.e: Mature insulin has only the A and B chains linked by disulphide bridges; the C peptide is not present.

questions.q: Over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are ______.
questions.e: Transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have also been produced, but mice form the vast majority.

questions.q: Transgenic mice are being developed for testing the safety of the ______ vaccine before it is used on humans.
questions.e: If successful, transgenic mice could replace monkeys for testing the safety of batches of the vaccine.

questions.q: Transgenic animals have been used to produce alpha-1-antitrypsin, a protein used to treat ______.
questions.e: Transgenic animals can produce useful biological products by introducing the gene that codes for the product.

questions.q: A single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule, which hybridises to its complementary DNA and is used to detect a mutated gene, is called a ______.
questions.e: The probe binds to its complementary DNA in a clone of cells, which is then detected by autoradiography.

questions.q: Answer the following about gene therapy and molecular diagnosis.
p: (a) In the first clinical gene therapy (1990), a functional ADA cDNA was introduced into the patient's lymphocytes using which type of vector?
retroviral|retrovirus|retroviral vector
(b) If the ADA gene from marrow cells is introduced into cells at early ______ stages, it could be a permanent cure.
embryonic|embryo
(c) ELISA is based on the principle of antigen-______ interaction.
antibody
questions.e: Genetically engineered lymphocytes are not immortal, so periodic infusion is needed; ELISA detects infection by the presence of antigens or of antibodies against the pathogen.

questions.q: The interaction in which both interacting species benefit is called ______.
questions.e: Lichens (fungus and alga) and mycorrhizae (fungus and plant roots) are examples of mutualism.

questions.q: The population interaction in which both interacting species are harmed is called ______.
questions.e: In competition the fitness of one species is lowered in the presence of another that shares limited resources.

questions.q: The size of a population is usually measured in terms of its ______, the number of individuals per unit area.
questions.e: Population density (N) changes through natality, mortality, immigration and emigration.

questions.q: The interaction in which one species is harmed and the other is unaffected is called ______.
questions.e: Amensalism is a (-, 0) interaction.

questions.q: An age pyramid with a broad base (triangular shape) indicates a(n) ______ population.
questions.e: A broad base shows many pre-reproductive individuals; a bell shape shows a stable population and an urn shape a declining one.

questions.q: In brood parasitism, the cuckoo (koel) lays its eggs in the nest of its host, the ______.
questions.e: The parasitic eggs resemble the host's eggs in size and colour, which reduces the chance of the host detecting and ejecting them.

questions.q: Gause's '______ exclusion principle' states that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely.
questions.e: According to Gause, the competitively inferior species will eventually be eliminated.

questions.q: Each fig species is pollinated only by its partner species of ______.
questions.e: The female wasp uses the fruit as an egg-laying site and pollinates the inflorescence; the developing seeds feed the larvae.

questions.q: On the rocky sea coasts of Scotland, the larger barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller barnacle ______.
questions.e: Connell's field experiments showed this competitive exclusion of Chthamalus by Balanus.

questions.q: When the predatory starfish ______ was removed from an American Pacific coast intertidal community, more than 10 species of invertebrates became extinct within a year.
questions.e: Without the predator, interspecific competition among the prey species increased and some were eliminated.

questions.q: A population with r = 0.1 per year and carrying capacity K = 1000 has 500 individuals. Using the logistic equation dN/dt = rN(K - N)/K, what is its growth rate (individuals per year)?
A population of 1000 deer in a forest had 60 births, 20 deaths, 10 immigrants and 5 emigrants during a year.
p: (a) What is the population size at the end of the year?
(b) What is the birth rate per deer per year?
(c) What is the number of births in a population during a given period called?
natality

questions.q: The rate of biomass production in an ecosystem is called ______.
questions.e: Productivity is expressed, for example, in g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹.

questions.q: The mass of living material at a trophic level at a particular time is called the ______.
questions.e: Standing crop is measured as the biomass of living organisms or their number per unit area.

questions.q: During decomposition, the accumulation of a dark coloured, amorphous substance that is highly resistant to microbial action is called ______.
questions.e: Humus decomposes at an extremely slow rate and, being colloidal, acts as a reservoir of nutrients.

questions.q: The degradation of humus by some microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients, is called ______.
questions.e: Mineralisation is the last step of decomposition.

questions.q: Of the annual net primary productivity of the biosphere, how much (in billion tons) is contributed by the oceans, even though they occupy about 70 per cent of the surface?
questions.e: Oceans contribute only about 55 of the 170 billion tons; the rest comes from land.

questions.q: Consider the food chain: grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> hawk.
p: (a) At which trophic level is the frog?
(b) Is the snake a secondary or a tertiary consumer?
tertiary|tertiary consumer
(c) If the grass fixes 10,000 J of energy, how much energy reaches the snake according to the 10 per cent law?
J
questions.e: Grass is the first trophic level, so the frog is the third and the snake (fourth level) is a tertiary consumer; 10,000 -> 1,000 -> 100 -> 10 J.

questions.q: Protecting biodiversity in its natural habitat, as in national parks and wildlife sanctuaries, is called ______ conservation.
questions.e: In situ conservation protects the whole ecosystem; ex situ conservation protects threatened species outside their habitat, as in zoos.

questions.q: The four major causes of biodiversity loss are collectively called the 'Evil ______'.
questions.e: The Evil Quartet: habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasions and co-extinctions.

questions.q: Preserving gametes of threatened species in viable and fertile condition for long periods at very low temperature is called ______.
questions.e: Gametes and embryos are preserved at -196 °C as an ex situ conservation strategy.

questions.q: Sacred groves are found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of which Indian state?
questions.e: Sacred groves also occur in the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan and the Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra.

questions.q: The historic Convention on Biological Diversity ('The Earth Summit') was held in Rio de Janeiro in which year?
questions.e: The 2002 World Summit on Sustainable Development in Johannesburg followed it, pledging to reduce the rate of biodiversity loss by 2010.

questions.q: In the species-area relationship, Z usually lies between 0.1 and 0.2. What is the value of Z found for frugivorous birds and mammals in tropical forests of different continents?
questions.e: When species-area relationships are analysed over very large areas such as entire continents, the slope becomes much steeper.

questions.q: Answer the following about the biodiversity of India.
p: (a) India has more than how many genetically different strains of rice?
(b) India has about how many varieties of mango?
(c) Which level of biodiversity do these varieties represent?
genetic|genetic diversity
questions.e: India has more than 50,000 strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango, showing genetic diversity within a species.
